deep.reconstruction:
The page is mostly a draft of a historical survey, with almost no mathematics. The machine transcription is very fragmentary; the reading below follows the image as far as possible.

(a) Top left, pencil: a heading reading roughly 'Dirichlet[?]. Zweit.[?] Lief.[?] 12'. It looks like a bibliographic or administrative reference, for example to a journal 'Lieferung' (instalment). Its exact reading is uncertain.

(b) Middle of the left sheet: a chain of small symbols linked by arcs. Some look like fractions or indices, some are circled, with signs between them. It is illegible and not reconstructible. It may be a scheme of index pairings or a mnemonic. I offer no interpretation.

(c) Lower right, the main text. It is a prose draft of the history of the vibrating-string problem and of trigonometric series. As far as legible, it says roughly:
- 'The general solution of the problem as against special solutions.'
- Taylor found, for a certain initial shape of the string, the vibrations, namely the sine-shaped mode z = a sin(n*pi*x/l) (times a time factor). The time factor is my completion.
- Then followed d'Alembert's solution, which in modern form is z = f(x+ct) + f(x-ct). That formula is mine; it is not written on the page.
- Euler [remarked/disputed] concerning the motions of the string.
- Daniel Bernoulli, 'almost simultaneously', gave his solution as a superposition of the simple modes, i.e. a trigonometric series.
- Euler disputed whether this superposition is general enough for arbitrary motions. The issue was continuity or arbitrariness of the initial shape, which could consist of separate pieces of curves ('eine Reihe einzelner ...').
- A further, unclear clause asks whether the branch/arc ('Zweig') belongs at the end.
- Separate paragraph: '40 years later Fourier first made the remark (Acad. ... VII) that an arbitrary function can be represented [by such a series].' The word 'Funktion' has a correction struck through.

This is essentially the same narrative as Section 1 of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published 1867). That section runs Taylor, d'Alembert, Euler, D. Bernoulli, Lagrange, Fourier. There Riemann writes that almost fifty years passed before Fourier's remark. The draft here says 40 years.

(d) Lower left: fragments of integral signs, an interval '(x_1 ... x_2)' and fractions. These hint at integrals over an interval, plausibly the Fourier coefficient integrals, but nothing can be reconstructed.

(e) Bottom right: names with street addresses, e.g. '... Lindenstr. 45', '... Dorotheen[str.] 83', '... 71'. These are Berlin streets, i.e. personal memoranda.

No derivation is carried out on the page.
errors: Chronology in the draft: it says Fourier's remark came '40 Jahre später'. Counting from Bernoulli (1753) to Fourier's first memoir (1807) gives about 54 years; counting from the Euler-Lagrange debate of the 1760s-70s gives about 40. The published Habilitationsschrift says 'fast fünfzig Jahre', so the figure was apparently revised.
Nothing else is checkable mathematically; no computational steps are present.

results.what: Historical outline of the vibrating-string controversy (Taylor's sine mode; d'Alembert's solution; Euler; D. Bernoulli's superposition; Fourier's claim that arbitrary functions are representable by trigonometric series)
results.modern_name: History of Fourier series / vibrating string controversy
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's own Habilitationsschrift (1854, publ. 1867), Section 1, is the classic account of this history

results.modern_name: Normal modes of the vibrating string

deep.surprise_reason: This is a preparatory draft of the historical introduction to Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series, which is well known. The only minor point of interest is the variant '40 Jahre' against the published 'fast fünfzig Jahre', showing the text was revised. There is no new mathematics.

transcription_corrections: Main text, lines 3-4: the formula reads like 'Taylor'sche war (z = a sin (n*pi/l) x)', i.e. a sine with argument proportional to x. It is not just '... war'.
'Hierauf folgte die d'Alembert'sche Lösung' appears legible; the name in the next line is likely 'Euler' or 'Daniel Bernoulli'. The phrase '(fast gleichzeitig)' is clear.
'40 Jahre später machte Fourier erst die Bemerkung' is clearly the opening of the second paragraph. '(Acad. VII)' is at the right margin, and 'Funktion' is struck through and replaced.
Heading: the reading 'Dirichlet' is doubtful; it may be another name or reference.
Bottom-right addresses: 'Lindenstr. 45' and 'Dorotheen[str.] 83' are Berlin streets; the third entry ends with '71'.
